blocks.content: This closing topic of the Kubernetes course pulls together the most important practices covered throughout, into one real, practical checklist worth applying to every manifest you actually write.
1. Always Set Resource Requests and Limits
blocks.text: 1. Always Set Resource Requests and Limits

blocks.content: Exactly as covered in the Namespaces & Resource Management module, every container should declare realistic requests and limits, without them, the scheduler cannot place Pods sensibly, and a single misbehaving container can affect its entire node.

blocks.alt: A foundational practice covered in its own dedicated module, worth applying to every container

blocks.content:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi

code.content:

  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi

codes.yaml:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m

  limits:

    memory: 512Mi

blocks.content: Exactly the genuinely critical practice covered in the Health Checks and Rolling Updates modules, a real, accurate readiness probe is foundational to actually achieving zero-downtime deployments, not an optional nicety.

blocks.alt: Genuinely critical, not optional, covered directly in the Rolling Updates module

blocks.content: 3. Prefer apply Over edit or create
blocks.text: 3. Prefer apply Over edit or create

blocks.content: Exactly the guidance covered throughout the kubectl module, apply's declarative, idempotent nature makes it the right default for real, ongoing workflows, reach for edit or create only for genuine, deliberate exceptions.

blocks.alt: The declarative default covered throughout the kubectl module, not an imperative shortcut

blocks.content: This connects directly to the real risk flagged in the edit topic, a live, un-tracked change can be silently overwritten the next time someone applies the original manifest, keeping every manifest in version control, and treating it as the actual source of truth, avoids that entirely.

blocks.alt: Avoiding the exact risk flagged directly in the kubectl module's edit topic

blocks.content: Consistent, deliberate labeling is what makes the selector mechanism, covered throughout this course, actually work correctly, and namespaces, covered in their own module, are the right tool for organizing a shared cluster among teams and environments.

blocks.alt: The two organizational practices that make everything else in this course actually work well together

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Resource requests and limits, a real readiness probe, preferring apply, version-controlled manifests, and consistent labeling are the practices that separate a fragile setup from a genuinely reliable one.
None of these are new ideas, they are the same practices covered throughout this entire course, gathered here as one final, practical checklist to actually apply.
